sections.title: Sounds and spelling
sections.summary: Bokmål uses the Latin alphabet plus æ, ø and å, and its spelling is fairly regular once you know a handful of silent letters and the kj/skj sounds. This chapter covers the pronunciation essentials, including vowel length and the two pitch accents.

rules.title: Three extra letters: æ, ø, å
rules.body: The Norwegian alphabet has 29 letters: the 26 English ones followed by æ, ø and å, in that order, so they come last in dictionaries. æ sounds like the a in English 'bad', usually held long: være, lære, sær. ø is a rounded e, like French 'peu' or German 'schön': øl, sønn, kjøre. å is like the aw in 'law' or the o in 'more': år, gå, måne. In old spellings and some names å is written aa (Haakon, Aasen).

rules.title: Long and short vowels
rules.body: Every stressed vowel is either long or short, and the spelling tells you which: a vowel followed by one consonant (or by nothing) is long, a vowel followed by two consonants is short. This can change meaning: tak (roof, long a) and takk (thanks, short a); lese (to read, long e) and lesse (to load); vin (wine) and vinn (win!). One exception: m is normally not doubled at the end of a word even after a short vowel: kom, rom, hjem, but komme, rommet when an ending follows.

rules.title: The vowels u, y and o
rules.body: Norwegian u is a tightly rounded vowel between English 'oo' and German 'ü': hus, du, ut. y is like German ü or French u: say 'ee' with rounded lips: by, ny, syk. The letter o is usually pronounced like the oo in 'moon': bok, god, sol, stor. But in many words with a short vowel it sounds like å instead: kopp, sommer, jobb, om, godt. An unstressed final -e is a weak 'uh' sound and is always pronounced, so jente, ikke and gate all have two syllables.

rules.title: Silent letters
rules.body: Several consonants are written but not spoken. d is usually silent at the end of a word after a long vowel or after l, n, r: god, brød, med, tid, land, kald, bord. The t is silent in det and in the neuter definite ending -et: huset, brødet, eplet (but the t of the past-tense ending -et is pronounced: snakket). h is silent before j and v: hjem, hjelpe, hva, hvor, hvit. g is silent in the endings -ig and -lig (ferdig, hyggelig, viktig) and before j (gjøre, gjerne, gjest). The word og (and) is pronounced like å, and the -eg of jeg, meg, deg, seg is pronounced like the diphthong ei.

rules.title: The kj and skj sounds
rules.body: kj is pronounced like the ch in German 'ich', a soft hiss with the tongue close to the hard palate: kjøkken, kjære, kjole, kjenne. A plain k before i or y takes the same sound: kino, kirke, kylling. The spellings skj, sj, and sk before i or y are all pronounced like English sh: skje, skjorte, sjø, sjokolade, ski, skip, sky. In Eastern Norwegian, rs is also pronounced sh: norsk, vers, Lars. Many younger speakers now merge kj into sh (so kjole sounds like 'sjole'); this is widespread but still treated as non-standard.

rules.title: Stress and unstressed prefixes
rules.body: Native words are stressed on the first syllable: SNAKke, LÆrer, ARbeide. Many loanwords keep the stress later in the word: stasJON, universiTET, teleFON, stuDENT, muSIKK. The prefixes be-, er- and for- are unstressed, so the stress falls on the next syllable: beTAle, forSTÅ, forTELle, erFAring. In compounds the first part carries the main stress: BUSSholdeplass, KAFfekopp.

examples.en: The train leaves from the station.

rules.title: Pitch accent (tonelag)
rules.body: Norwegian words carry one of two melodies. Tone 1 is a simple rise; tone 2 starts higher, dips and then rises. Only words of two or more syllables can have tone 2, and a few pairs are told apart by tone alone: bønder (farmers, tone 1) and bønner (beans, tone 2); tanken (the tank, tone 1) and tanken (the thought, tone 2); hender (hands, tone 1) and hender (happens, tone 2). Roughly, a one-syllable word plus an ending (huset, bilen) keeps tone 1, while words with two syllables in their basic form (jente, snakke) have tone 2. The melodies vary by dialect and mistakes rarely cause misunderstanding, so listen and copy rather than worry.

rules.title: Diphthongs and the letter r
rules.body: Three diphthongs are common. ei, as in nei, hei, reise, sounds like the ai in English 'aisle' but starting from an æ sound. au, as in sau and august, is roughly 'eh-oo'. øy, as in øy, høy, gøy, starts with ø and glides to y. ai appears in a few words such as hai and kai. The letter r is a tongue-tip trill or tap in Eastern Norwegian and a throaty uvular r in the south-west (Bergen, Stavanger). In Eastern Norwegian, r merges with a following t, d, n, l or s into a single retroflex sound: bort, barn, ferdig, norsk.

rules.title: Rare letters and the sound ng
rules.body: The letters c, q, w, x and z appear only in loanwords and names: camping, Qatar, Wenche, taxi, zoo. w is pronounced like v, z like s, and c like s or k depending on the word. The combination ng is one nasal sound with no separate g, as in English 'sing': lang, penger, mange, Norge. Spelling reforms replaced most foreign spellings with Norwegian ones: sentrum (centre), sjokolade (chocolate), stasjon (station), kvalitet (quality).

exercises.explain: The g of og is silent and the o sounds like å, so og sounds just like å.

exercises.explain: å is a rounded back vowel like the aw in law or the o in more.

exercises.explain: A vowel before a double consonant is short, so takk has a short a and tak a long one.

exercises.explain: The t of the neuter definite ending -et is silent: huset sounds like 'huse'.

exercises.explain: Both are pronounced with the same sounds; bønder has tone 1 and bønner tone 2.

exercises.explain: Tone 2 needs two syllables for its dip-and-rise melody; one-syllable words always have tone 1.

exercises.explain: lese has a single consonant after the stressed e, so the e is long; the others have double consonants and short vowels.

exercises.explain: r plus s merges into a retroflex sh sound in Eastern Norwegian: norsk, vers, Lars.

exercises.explain: vin (wine) has a long i and vinn (win!) a short one; the other pairs differ in endings or vowels.

sections.title: Nouns, gender and articles
sections.summary: Norwegian nouns belong to one of three genders, and 'the' is a suffix glued onto the noun rather than a separate word. This chapter covers en/ei/et, the definite endings -en/-a/-et, and the plurals in -er and -ene.

rules.title: Three genders
rules.body: Every noun is masculine, feminine or neuter, and the gender shows in the indefinite article: en bil (a car), ei jente (a girl), et hus (a house). Gender is mostly unpredictable, so learn each noun with its article. Some tendencies help: words for male people are masculine, words for female people are feminine, nouns ending in -het, -else, -sjon and -ing are masculine (en nyhet, en følelse, en stasjon, en regning), and nouns ending in -eri, -ment and -um are neuter (et bakeri, et argument, et museum). Roughly half of all nouns are masculine, a quarter feminine and a quarter neuter.

rules.title: The feminine is optional
rules.body: Bokmål allows every feminine noun to be treated as masculine: ei jente or en jente, jenta or jenten, ei bok or en bok. Formal and conservative Bokmål uses en and -en for nearly everything, while everyday speech in most of Norway uses ei and -a for common feminine words: jenta, boka, hytta, kua, døra. Both styles are correct; choose one and be consistent. Some nouns are nearly always feminine in daily usage: jente, kone, hytte, ku, geit, øy, and the definite form boka.

examples.en: The girl is reading the book. (also: Jenten leser boken.)

examples.target: Vi har ei hytte på fjellet.
examples.en: We have a cabin in the mountains.

rules.title: The indefinite article, and when to drop it
rules.body: en, ei and et go before the noun like English a/an: en kopp, et eple. There is no article after 'er' when you state a profession, nationality or religion: Hun er lærer. Han er nordmann. Jeg er student. The article comes back when an adjective is added: Hun er en god lærer. Many set phrases with 'ha' also drop the article: Jeg har bil (I have a car), Har du barn? (Do you have children?).

examples.target: Jeg vil ha en kopp kaffe.
examples.en: I would like a cup of coffee.

rules.title: The definite singular is a suffix
rules.body: English puts 'the' in front of the noun; Norwegian attaches it to the end: bil becomes bilen, jente becomes jenta (or jenten), hus becomes huset, eple becomes eplet. If the noun already ends in -e, only -n or -t is added: gate becomes gaten or gata, eple becomes eplet. The t of neuter -et is silent, so huset sounds like 'huse'. Nouns ending in -er or -el simply add -en: læreren, sykkelen, vinteren.

examples.en: The girl is ten years old.

rules.title: Indefinite plural: -er
rules.body: Most nouns form the plural with -er: bil becomes biler, dag becomes dager, stol becomes stoler. Nouns that already end in -e just add -r: jenter, gater, uker. Neuter nouns of one syllable take no ending at all: et hus, to hus; et barn, tre barn; et år, fem år; et bord, mange bord. Neuter nouns of more than one syllable take -er as usual: epler, vinduer. Nouns in -er that denote people add only -e: en lærer, to lærere; en baker, to bakere. Nouns in -el and -er usually drop the e before the ending: sykkel becomes sykler, vinter becomes vintrer, søster becomes søstre.

rules.title: Definite plural: -ene
rules.body: The definite plural ends in -ene for nearly all nouns, whatever the gender: bilene, jentene, husene, eplene, årene. Nouns in -er that denote people drop an e: lærerne, bakerne. A few neuter nouns prefer the ending -a in the definite plural: barna (the children) and beina (the legs) are much more common than barnene and beinene, although both are allowed. Neuter one-syllable nouns, which have no ending in the indefinite plural, still take -ene in the definite plural: hus, husene; bord, bordene.

rules.title: Irregular plurals
rules.body: A small group of common nouns changes its vowel in the plural, much like English man/men: mann, menn, mennene; bok, bøker, bøkene; hånd, hender, hendene; fot, føtter, føttene; tann, tenner, tennene; natt, netter, nettene; tre, trær, trærne. Family words have their own forms: bror, brødre; far, fedre; mor, mødre; datter, døtre. øye (eye) becomes øyne, øynene. Some masculine nouns take no plural ending: en sko, to sko, skoene; en ting, mange ting, tingene; en feil, flere feil; en mus, to mus.

rules.title: Double definiteness
rules.body: After the demonstratives den, det, de (that, those) and denne, dette, disse (this, these), the noun still takes its definite ending: den bilen (that car), det huset, de bilene, denne boka, dette eplet, disse barna. The same happens when an adjective comes between (den nye bilen, see chapter 6) and when a possessive follows the noun (bilen min, see chapter 3). Norwegian also uses the definite form for body parts where English uses my/your: Jeg vasker hendene, Han har vondt i hodet. General statements have no article, as in English: Jeg liker kaffe.

rules.title: Compound nouns
rules.body: Norwegian writes compounds as one word, and the last part decides the gender and the plural: en fotball + et lag gives et fotballag, en kaffe + en kopp gives en kaffekopp, et barn + en hage gives en barnehage. Sometimes a linking -s or -e joins the parts: et arbeid + et rom gives et arbeidsrom, en jul + et tre gives et juletre. Writing a compound as two words changes the meaning, as in the well-known lammekoteletter (lamb chops) versus lamme koteletter (lame chops).

sections.title: Pronouns and possession
sections.summary: Norwegian pronouns have a subject form and an object form, possessives agree with the thing owned, and a special reflexive possessive 'sin' shows that something belongs to the subject. This chapter covers jeg/meg, du/deg, han/hun, min/mi/mitt and sin.

rules.title: Subject pronouns
rules.body: The subject forms are jeg (I), du (you, one person), han (he), hun (she), den/det (it), vi (we), dere (you, several people), de (they). de is pronounced 'di'. The verb never changes with the person, so jeg er, du er, hun er, vi er. det also serves as a dummy subject like English 'it' or 'there': Det regner (It is raining), Det er kaldt (It is cold).

rules.title: Object pronouns
rules.body: After a verb or a preposition the pronouns change: meg (me), deg (you), ham (him; han is also accepted as an object form), henne (her), den/det (it), oss (us), dere (you, plural), dem (them). Only dere has the same form as subject and object. Jeg ser deg (I see you). Hun elsker ham (She loves him). Kan du hjelpe oss? (Can you help us?).

rules.title: 'it': den or det
rules.body: When 'it' refers back to a noun, choose by gender: den for masculine and feminine nouns, det for neuter nouns. Bilen er ny. Jeg liker den. Huset er stort. Jeg liker det. Boka? Den er god. When 'it' does not refer to a particular noun, or refers to a whole idea, use det: Det er sant (That is true), Det er kaldt i dag.

examples.target: Bilen er ny. Jeg liker den.
examples.en: The car is new. I like it.

examples.target: Huset er stort. Jeg liker det.
examples.en: The house is big. I like it.

rules.title: Possessives agree with the thing owned
rules.body: The possessives for I and you have three or four forms that match the gender and number of the noun: min, mi, mitt, mine (my); din, di, ditt, dine (your). mi and di are used only with feminine nouns in their -a form (boka mi); with boken you say boken min. vår, vårt, våre (our) has three forms. hans (his), hennes (her), deres (your plural, and their) never change. So: bilen min, boka mi, huset mitt, barna mine; bilen hans, huset hennes, barna deres.

rules.title: Where the possessive goes
rules.body: The everyday pattern puts the possessive after the noun, and the noun takes its definite form: bilen min, huset ditt, boka hennes, foreldrene våre. The possessive can also go before the noun, which then stays indefinite: min bil, ditt hus, hennes bok. This order is more formal or emphatic, and it is the normal choice with some words such as family: min mor, min bror are as common as moren min, broren min.

rules.title: The reflexive possessive sin, si, sitt, sine
rules.body: In the third person Norwegian distinguishes between the subject's own things and someone else's. sin, si, sitt, sine (his own, her own, its own, their own) refer back to the subject of the same clause: Han vasker bilen sin (He washes his own car). hans, hennes, deres point to someone else: Han vasker bilen hans (He washes another man's car). sin agrees with the noun like min: bilen sin, boka si, huset sitt, barna sine. Because sin must refer to a subject, it can never be part of the subject itself: 'his brother is coming' is Broren hans kommer, never Broren sin kommer.

rules.title: Reflexive pronouns and 'each other'
rules.body: When the object is the same person as the subject, use the reflexive forms: jeg vasker meg, du vasker deg, han/hun/de vasker seg, vi vasker oss, dere vasker dere. Only the third person has a special form, seg, used for han, hun, den, det and de. Many everyday verbs are reflexive in Norwegian: å sette seg (sit down), å legge seg (go to bed), å skynde seg (hurry), å glede seg til (look forward to), å kose seg (enjoy oneself), å føle seg (feel). 'Each other' is hverandre: De elsker hverandre.

examples.en: I go to bed at eleven.
We are looking forward to the holiday.

rules.title: Demonstratives: this and that
rules.body: 'This' is denne with masculine and feminine nouns, dette with neuter nouns, and disse in the plural. 'That' is den, det and de. The noun that follows always takes its definite form: denne bilen, dette huset, disse barna, den boka, det eplet, de jentene. Standing alone, dette and det mean 'this' and 'that' in general: Hva er dette? (What is this?), Det er bra (That is good).

rules.title: Addressing people and the generic 'one'
rules.body: Modern Norwegian uses du to everyone, including strangers, shop staff and bosses. The polite De (with object Dem and possessive Deres, capitalised) survives only in very formal letters and when addressing the royal family, so you can ignore it in practice. For a general 'one' or 'you' as the subject, use man (or en): Man kan ikke vite alt (One cannot know everything). As an object the generic pronoun is en: Det gjør en glad.

examples.en: Can you help me? (said even to a stranger)

sections.title: Verbs in the present and infinitive
sections.summary: Norwegian verbs are refreshingly simple: the present tense has one form for all persons, and the infinitive is marked by å. This chapter also introduces the modal verbs kan, vil, må and skal, which are followed by a bare infinitive.

rules.title: The infinitive with å
rules.body: The dictionary form of a verb is the infinitive, usually ending in -e and introduced by the marker å (to): å snakke (to speak), å spise (to eat), å lese (to read), å komme (to come). Verbs of one syllable that end in a stressed vowel have no -e: å bo (to live), å gå (to go), å se (to see), å ha (to have), å si (to say), å tro (to believe). å is pronounced like the letter å, and it is written only with the infinitive, never with other verb forms.

rules.title: The present tense: add -r
rules.body: The present is formed by adding -r to the infinitive, and the same form is used for every person: jeg snakker, du snakker, han snakker, vi snakker, dere snakker, de snakker. å spise gives spiser, å bo gives bor, å gå gives går, å komme gives kommer. There is no separate progressive form, so jeg leser means both 'I read' and 'I am reading'.

rules.title: Irregular present forms
rules.body: A few very common verbs do not simply add -r. å være (to be) has er; å gjøre (to do) has gjør; å vite (to know a fact) has vet; å spørre (to ask) has spør; å si (to say) has sier. The modal verbs have short present forms: å kunne gives kan, å ville gives vil, å måtte gives må, å skulle gives skal, å burde gives bør. å ha (to have) is regular: har.

examples.en: She says that she is coming.

rules.title: What the present is used for
rules.body: The present covers what is happening now (Jeg spiser), habits (Jeg spiser frokost klokka sju) and, with a time expression, the future (Jeg reiser i morgen, I am leaving tomorrow). To stress that something is going on right now, Norwegian uses little constructions instead of an -ing form: Jeg holder på å lese (I am in the middle of reading), Jeg sitter og leser (I am sitting reading), Han står og venter, De driver og pusser opp (They are busy renovating).

rules.title: Modal verbs: kan, vil, må, skal, bør
rules.body: The modals are followed by the bare infinitive without å: Jeg kan svømme (I can swim), Du må komme (You must come). kan means can or is able to; må means must or has to; skal means shall, is going to, and is used for plans and promises; bør means ought to or should. Beware of vil: it means 'wants to', not English 'will': Jeg vil ha kaffe means I want coffee. For future 'will', use skal or the present (see below). få + infinitive means to get to or be allowed to: Jeg får komme (I am allowed to come).

examples.target: Jeg vil ha en kopp te.
examples.en: I want a cup of tea.
We are going to travel to Bergen.

rules.title: Modals without a main verb
rules.body: When the meaning is movement to a place, Norwegian happily drops the verb of motion after a modal: Jeg skal hjem (I am going home), Jeg må på jobb (I have to go to work), Vi skal til Spania i sommer, Kan du ut i kveld? (Can you go out tonight?). Similarly vil is used alone with an object in Vil du ha kaffe? (Do you want coffee?), where ha is the main verb. These short sentences are normal, not sloppy.

examples.en: She has to go to work.

examples.target: Vi skal til Spania i sommer.
examples.en: We are going to Spain this summer.

rules.title: Verbs that take å + infinitive
rules.body: Most verbs other than the modals link to a following verb with å: liker å, prøver å (try to), begynner å (begin to), pleier å (usually do), lærer å, husker å, trenger å (need to; the å is often dropped after trenger ikke), har lyst til å (feel like). Purpose is expressed with for å (in order to): Jeg går på jobb for å tjene penger. 'Without ...ing' is uten å: uten å spørre.

examples.en: She is trying to learn Norwegian.

examples.target: Jeg pleier å stå opp klokka sju.
examples.en: I usually get up at seven.

examples.target: Vi går på jobb for å tjene penger.
examples.en: We go to work in order to earn money.

examples.target: Har du lyst til å gå på kino?
examples.en: Do you feel like going to the cinema?

rules.title: Verbs ending in -s
rules.body: A group of verbs ends in -s in all their forms, with a present in -es or -s: å trives, jeg trives (I like it here, I am happy here); å finnes, det finnes (there is, there exists); å synes, jeg synes (I think, in the sense of having an opinion); å møtes, vi møtes (we meet each other); å lykkes (succeed); å minnes (remember). Note the difference between synes (opinion) and tror (believe something uncertain): Jeg synes filmen er god, but Jeg tror det blir regn.

examples.target: Jeg synes at filmen er god.
examples.en: I think the film is good.

rules.title: Talking about the future
rules.body: There are three common ways to express the future. The plain present with a time expression is the simplest: Jeg kommer i morgen. skal + infinitive expresses plans, intentions and promises: Jeg skal ringe deg. kommer til å + infinitive expresses predictions about what will happen regardless of anyone's will: Det kommer til å regne (It is going to rain), Du kommer til å like det. Remember that vil means 'want', not 'will'.

examples.target: Vi skal gifte oss i juni.
examples.en: We are getting married in June.

examples.target: Du kommer til å like det.

exercises.q: The infinitive marker 'to' in Norwegian is:
exercises.explain: The infinitive is introduced by å: å snakke.

exercises.q: The present tense of 'å snakke' is:
exercises.explain: The present adds -r to the infinitive: snakker.

exercises.q: The present tense has the same form for all persons.
exercises.explain: jeg snakker, du snakker, de snakker: no endings change with the person.
Present tense: infinitive snakke plus -r.

exercises.q: Vi ___ (live, from å bo) i Oslo.
exercises.explain: å bo has no -e, so the present is just bor.
er is the present of å være for every person, including de.

exercises.q: 'Jeg reiser i morgen' uses the present tense to talk about the future.
exercises.explain: With a time expression like i morgen, the present is a normal way to express the future.
vil means 'want to', not English 'will'.
kan is the present of å kunne and takes a bare infinitive.

exercises.q: After a modal verb such as må or kan, the next verb is:
exercises.explain: Modals take the infinitive without å: Jeg må gå.

exercises.q: Vi ___ (are going to, from å skulle) reise til Bergen i sommer.
exercises.explain: skal expresses plans and intentions.

exercises.q: 'Jeg skal hjem' is wrong because it has no main verb.
exercises.explain: With a direction, the verb of motion is normally dropped after a modal: Jeg skal hjem is perfectly correct.

exercises.q: Which sentence correctly asks 'What are you doing (right now)?' with a progressive construction?
exercises.explain: holde på med + noun or holde på å + verb expresses an ongoing activity.
liker is not a modal, so the following infinitive needs å.

exercises.en: She is trying to learn Norwegian.

options: I like it here, I am happy here
exercises.explain: å trives is an -s verb meaning to thrive or feel at home.

exercises.q: 'å synes' means to think in the sense of having an opinion.
exercises.explain: Jeg synes filmen er god gives an opinion; tror would express belief about something uncertain.

exercises.q: Det ___ (exist, from å finnes) mange dialekter i Norge.
exercises.explain: Det finnes means 'there is / there are'; fins is an accepted short form.

exercises.q: 'It is going to rain' using 'kommer til å':
exercises.explain: The prediction future is kommer til å + infinitive.

exercises.answer: Jeg går på jobb for å tjene penger.
exercises.en: I go to work in order to earn money.

exercises.q: Jeg sitter ___ leser. (the little word that links 'sits' and 'reads' in the progressive construction)
exercises.explain: sitter og leser literally 'sits and reads' expresses an ongoing action.

exercises.q: 'vil' is the normal way to form the future, like English 'will'.
exercises.explain: vil means 'want to'; the future uses skal, kommer til å or the present.

options: Hun kan ikke komme i dag.
Hun kan ikke å komme i dag.
Hun kan ikke kommer i dag.
Hun kan ikke komme i dag å.
exercises.explain: A modal is followed by the bare infinitive komme, with no å and no -r.
å gjøre has the irregular present gjør.

exercises.q: 'Jeg pleier å stå opp klokka sju' means:
options: I usually get up at seven
I plan to get up at seven
I must get up at seven
I would like to get up at seven
exercises.explain: å pleie å expresses a habit: what one usually does.

sections.title: Past tense and perfect
sections.summary: Norwegian has weak verbs that add -et, -te, -de or -dde in the past and strong verbs that change their vowel. The perfect uses har plus the past participle. This chapter shows the four weak groups, the common strong verbs, and when to choose the simple past or the perfect.

rules.title: Weak verbs, group 1: -et
rules.body: The largest group adds -et in the past and has the same form as the past participle: å snakke, snakket, har snakket; å vaske, vasket, har vasket; å jobbe, jobbet, har jobbet; å kaste, kastet, har kastet. These verbs typically have a stem ending in two consonants (snakk-, jobb-, vask-, elsk-). The ending -a (snakka, jobba) is an accepted and common alternative in speech and informal writing.

examples.target: Jeg snakket med henne i går.

rules.title: Weak verbs, group 2: -te
rules.body: Verbs whose stem ends in a single consonant such as l, s, p, k, n, r, or in a double consonant such as ll, mm, nn, often take -te in the past and -t in the participle: å kjøpe, kjøpte, har kjøpt; å lese, leste, har lest; å spise, spiste, har spist; å reise, reiste, har reist; å tenke, tenkte, har tenkt; å glemme, glemte, har glemt; å kjenne, kjente, har kjent; å høre, hørte, har hørt. A few irregular weak verbs also belong here: å spørre, spurte, har spurt; å selge, solgte, har solgt; å fortelle, fortalte, har fortalt; å velge, valgte, har valgt.

rules.title: Weak verbs, groups 3 and 4: -de and -dde
rules.body: Verbs whose stem ends in v, g or a diphthong take -de in the past and -d in the participle: å leve, levde, har levd; å prøve, prøvde, har prøvd; å bygge, bygde, har bygd; å pleie, pleide, har pleid; å eie, eide, har eid. One-syllable verbs ending in a stressed vowel take -dde and -dd: å bo, bodde, har bodd; å tro, trodde, har trodd; å nå, nådde, har nådd; å sy, sydde, har sydd; å snu, snudde, har snudd.

examples.target: Vi bodde i Bergen i fem år.
examples.en: We lived in Bergen for five years.
I thought you were at home.

examples.target: De har bygd et nytt hus.
examples.en: They have built a new house.

rules.title: Strong verbs: vowel change, no ending
rules.body: Strong verbs mark the past by changing the vowel and take no ending: å drikke, drakk, har drukket; å finne, fant, har funnet; å skrive, skrev, har skrevet; å komme, kom, har kommet; å gå, gikk, har gått; å se, så, har sett; å få, fikk, har fått; å ta, tok, har tatt; å gi, ga, har gitt; å stå, sto, har stått; å sitte, satt, har sittet; å ligge, lå, har ligget; å sove, sov, har sovet; å synge, sang, har sunget; å hjelpe, hjalp, har hjulpet; å bli, ble, har blitt. The participle usually ends in -et or -tt. Learn the common strong verbs as sets of three.

rules.title: The most irregular verbs
rules.body: A handful of everyday verbs must simply be memorised: å være, var, har vært (be); å ha, hadde, har hatt (have); å gjøre, gjorde, har gjort (do); å si, sa, har sagt (say); å vite, visste, har visst (know); å legge, la, har lagt (lay, put); å sette, satte, har satt (set); å treffe, traff, har truffet (meet); å spørre, spurte, har spurt (ask); å bringe, brakte, har brakt (bring). Note that satt is both the past of sitte and the participle of sette.

examples.en: What did you do at the weekend?

examples.target: Hun sa at hun var trett.
examples.en: She said that she was tired.

rules.title: The perfect: har + past participle
rules.body: The perfect is formed with har and the past participle, for every verb including verbs of motion: Jeg har spist, Hun har kommet, De har reist. (er kommet and er blitt also exist for a resulting state, but har is always safe.) The participle never changes. Use the perfect when the time is not stated and the action matters now: Jeg har mistet nøklene (I have lost my keys); for experiences: Har du vært i Norge?; and for things that began in the past and still continue: Jeg har bodd her i to år (I have lived here for two years, and still do).

examples.target: Har du noen gang vært i Norge?
examples.en: Have you ever been to Norway?

examples.target: Hun har bodd her i to år.
examples.en: She has lived here for two years.

rules.title: Simple past or perfect?
rules.body: The simple past (preteritum) is used whenever a finished time is mentioned or understood: i går, i fjor, forrige uke, da jeg var liten, klokka åtte. Jeg så filmen i går, never Jeg har sett filmen i går. Compare Jeg bodde i Oslo i to år (I lived there for two years, and no longer do) with Jeg har bodd i Oslo i to år (I still live there). The perfect also appears with uncompleted periods such as i dag and i år: Jeg har ikke spist i dag. 'Used to' is pleide å: Jeg pleide å spille fotball.

examples.target: Vi bodde i Oslo i to år.
examples.en: We lived in Oslo for two years (not any more).

rules.title: The pluperfect: hadde + participle
rules.body: To describe something that had already happened before another past event, use hadde plus the past participle: Da jeg kom hjem, hadde hun allerede gått (When I came home, she had already left). Jeg hadde aldri sett snø før jeg kom til Norge. The structure mirrors the perfect, with hadde replacing har.

examples.target: Da jeg kom, hadde de spist.
examples.en: When I arrived, they had eaten.

examples.target: Hun hadde aldri vært i Oslo før.
examples.en: She had never been to Oslo before.

rules.title: Modal verbs in the past
rules.body: The modals have past forms that look like their infinitives: kan, kunne (could); vil, ville (wanted to); må, måtte (had to); skal, skulle (was going to); bør, burde (ought to have). Jeg kunne ikke komme i går. Hun ville ikke spise. Vi måtte gå. skulle is also used for the future seen from the past: Han sa at han skulle ringe (He said he would call). The participles are kunnet, villet, måttet, skullet, burdet: Jeg har ikke kunnet sove.

examples.target: Jeg kunne ikke komme i går.

examples.en: She did not want to eat.
We had to wait a long time.

examples.target: Han sa at han skulle ringe.
examples.en: He said that he would call.

exercises.q: The past tense of 'å snakke' is:
exercises.explain: snakke belongs to the largest weak group and takes -et (or -a).

exercises.q: The past tense of 'å kjøpe' is:
exercises.explain: kjøpe takes -te: kjøpte, har kjøpt.

exercises.q: Weak verbs form the past with an ending, while strong verbs change their vowel and take no ending.
exercises.explain: Compare snakket (weak) with drakk (strong).
snakke takes -et in the past; -a is an accepted alternative.

exercises.q: Hun ___ (read, past of å lese) boka i går.
exercises.explain: lese takes -te: leste.

exercises.q: The past tense of 'å bo' is:
exercises.explain: One-syllable verbs ending in a stressed vowel take -dde: bodde.

exercises.answer: Vi bodde i Bergen i fem år.
exercises.en: We lived in Bergen for five years.

exercises.q: The past tense of 'å gå' is 'gådde'.
exercises.explain: gå is a strong verb: gikk, har gått.
The strong verb gå has the past gikk.

exercises.q: The past tense of 'å være' is:
exercises.explain: være is irregular: var in the past, vært as participle.
The past of er is var.

exercises.q: The perfect tense is formed with:
exercises.explain: har is the auxiliary for all verbs: Jeg har spist, Hun har kommet.

exercises.answer: Jeg har bodd her i to år.
exercises.en: I have lived here for two years.

exercises.explain: spise takes -te in the past and -t in the participle: spist.

exercises.q: 'Jeg har sett filmen i går' is correct Norwegian.
exercises.explain: With a finished time like i går, the simple past is required: Jeg så filmen i går.

exercises.q: Har du ___ Norge? (Have you been to Norway?)
exercises.explain: The perfect needs the participle vært, and 'been to a country' uses i.
The participle of drikke is drukket.

exercises.q: 'Jeg bodde i Oslo i to år' implies that:
exercises.explain: The simple past presents the period as finished; har bodd would mean I still live there.

exercises.q: 'Da jeg kom hjem, hadde hun allerede gått' uses the pluperfect.
exercises.explain: hadde + participle describes something that happened before another past event.

exercises.answer: Da jeg kom, hadde de spist.
exercises.en: When I arrived, they had eaten.

exercises.q: Jeg ___ (could, past of kan) ikke komme i går.
exercises.explain: The past of kan is kunne, identical to its infinitive.
måtte is the past; måttet is the participle.

exercises.q: 'Jeg pleide å spille fotball' means 'I used to play football'.
exercises.explain: pleide å, the past of pleie å, expresses a former habit.

exercises.q: Hun ___ (said, past of å si) at hun var trett.
exercises.explain: si is irregular: sa, har sagt.

exercises.answer: Har du noen gang vært i Norge?
exercises.en: Have you ever been to Norway?

exercises.explain: The perfect uses har plus the participle spist, and aldri goes after har.

exercises.q: Hvor lenge har du ___ (lived) i Norge?
exercises.explain: The participle of bo is bodd.

sections.title: Adjectives and agreement
sections.summary: Norwegian adjectives change their ending to match the noun: nothing for masculine and feminine, -t for neuter, -e for plural and definite forms. This chapter also covers the comparative in -ere and superlative in -est, and the irregular forms you meet daily.

rules.title: Basic agreement: -, -t, -e
rules.body: An adjective takes no ending with a masculine or feminine noun in the singular (en stor bil, ei stor jente), -t with a neuter noun (et stort hus), and -e in the plural whatever the gender (store biler, store hus). The same endings apply when the adjective stands after er or blir: Bilen er stor. Huset er stort. Bilene er store. Learning the gender of each noun therefore pays off twice.

rules.title: The definite form: -e
rules.body: When the noun is definite, the adjective takes -e in all genders and numbers, and a front article den, det or de is added as well as the suffix on the noun: den store bilen, det store huset, de store bilene. This 'double definiteness' is standard Bokmål. The same -e form is used after possessives and demonstratives: min nye bil, den nye bilen min, denne gamle boka, dette lille huset.

rules.title: Adjectives that do not take -t
rules.body: Some adjectives are unchanged in the neuter. Those ending in -ig and -lig: et hyggelig hus, et viktig møte, et billig hotell. Those ending in -sk for nationalities and other derived adjectives: et norsk flagg, et typisk svar. Those ending in -e: et moderne hus, et stille rom. Those ending in a consonant plus -t: et kort brev, et svart bord. A few others such as glad and redd: et glad barn. Adjectives ending in a stressed vowel take -tt instead of -t: ny gives nytt, fri gives fritt, blå gives blått, grå gives grått.

rules.title: Small spelling changes
rules.body: Adjectives ending in -el, -en or -er drop the e when -e is added: gammel, gammelt, gamle; sulten, sultent, sultne; vakker, vakkert, vakre. A double consonant is simplified before -t in adjectives ending in -nn or -mm: grønn, grønt, grønne; tynn, tynt, tynne; dum, dumt, dumme (note that dum has one m but doubles it before -e). Adjectives already ending in -t or -tt are unchanged in the neuter: et kort brev, et svart bord, et flott hus.

examples.target: en gammel mann, et gammelt hus, gamle hus
examples.en: an old man, an old house, old houses

rules.title: Irregular: liten, egen, annen
rules.body: liten (small) is the most irregular adjective: en liten bil, ei lita jente, et lite hus, små biler in the plural, and lille in the definite singular: den lille bilen, det lille huset, de små husene. egen (own) goes egen, eget, egne: min egen bil, mitt eget hus, mine egne barn. annen (other, second) goes annen, anna (or annen), annet, andre: en annen dag, et annet sted, andre folk.

rules.title: Comparative -ere and superlative -est
rules.body: Most adjectives add -ere for the comparative and -est for the superlative: pen, penere, penest; billig, billigere, billigst (adjectives in -ig take only -st); varm, varmere, varmest. Adjectives in -el, -en, -er drop the e: enkel, enklere, enklest; vakker, vakrere, vakrest. Long adjectives, those ending in -e, -sk or -et, and participles use mer and mest instead: mer moderne, mest interessant, mer spennende, mer praktisk. The superlative takes -e when it stands before a definite noun: den peneste bilen, det billigste hotellet, den mest interessante boka.

examples.target: Filmen var mer interessant enn boka.
examples.en: The film was more interesting than the book.

examples.target: Hun er den mest moderne kunstneren.
examples.en: She is the most modern artist.

rules.title: Irregular comparison
rules.body: A set of common adjectives has irregular forms: god (or bra), bedre, best; dårlig, dårligere or verre, dårligst or verst; stor, større, størst; liten, mindre, minst; gammel, eldre, eldst; ung, yngre, yngst; lang, lengre, lengst; tung, tyngre, tyngst; få, færre, færrest; mange, flere, flest; mye, mer, mest; nær, nærmere, nærmest. These are used constantly, so learn them as sets of three.

examples.en: She is the oldest in the class.

examples.target: Jeg har flere bøker enn deg.
examples.en: I have more books than you.

rules.title: Making comparisons
rules.body: 'Than' is enn: Han er eldre enn meg (object form after enn is normal in speech; enn jeg is also correct). 'As ... as' is like ... som: Hun er like høy som broren sin. 'Not as ... as' is ikke så ... som. 'The more ... the more' is jo ... jo or jo ... desto: Jo mer jeg leser, jo mer lærer jeg. A superlative used after er takes no ending (Hun er eldst), but takes -e with the article (Hun er den eldste). 'Of' after a superlative is av: den største av dem.

examples.target: Hun er like høy som broren sin.
examples.en: She is as tall as her brother.

examples.target: Jo mer jeg leser, jo mer lærer jeg.
examples.en: The more I read, the more I learn.

examples.target: Dette er den beste filmen jeg har sett.
examples.en: This is the best film I have seen.

rules.title: Adjectives as adverbs
rules.body: The neuter form of an adjective, with -t, doubles as the adverb: Hun synger pent (She sings nicely), Han kjører fort, Jeg sover godt (godt is the neuter of god), Snakk langsomt. Adjectives that take no -t are unchanged as adverbs: Hun snakker tydelig. After verbs like være, bli and se ut, the adjective agrees with the subject as usual: Huset ser stort ut (The house looks big), Barna ble trette.

exercises.explain: hus is neuter, so the adjective takes -t.
Masculine singular indefinite takes no ending: en ny bil.

exercises.q: In the plural, adjectives take -e whatever the gender: 'store biler', 'store hus'.
exercises.explain: The plural ending -e is the same for all three genders.
bil is masculine, so the adjective has no ending after er.
hus is neuter, so the adjective takes -t even after er.
Definite: front article den, adjective in -e, noun with its suffix -en.
After det the adjective takes the definite -e: det nye huset.

exercises.q: After 'den/det/de' the adjective takes -e and the noun keeps its definite ending.
exercises.explain: This is double definiteness: den store bilen.
Adjectives ending in -ig and -lig take no -t: et hyggelig hus.
Adjectives ending in a stressed vowel take -tt: et nytt hus.
blå ends in a stressed vowel, so the neuter is blått.
Adjectives ending in -e, like moderne and stille, never take -t, so no ending is added in the neuter.
Adjectives in -el drop the e and simplify the double consonant before -e: gamle.
sulten drops its e before the plural -e: sultne.
liten is irregular: liten, lita, lite, små.
The plural of liten is the separate word små.

exercises.answer: Vi bor i et lite hus.
exercises.en: We live in a small house.

exercises.explain: Short adjectives add -ere; penest is the superlative.
stor has the irregular comparative større.
god is irregular: god, bedre, best.
Long adjectives use mest, and the adjective takes -e before a definite noun.

exercises.q: Hun er ___ (oldest; from gammel) i klassen.
exercises.explain: gammel has the irregular superlative eldst, used without -e after er.
Equality is expressed with like ... som.
The neuter form with -t serves as the adverb.

exercises.q: Jo mer jeg leser, ___ mer lærer jeg. (the more ... the more)
exercises.explain: The pattern is jo ... jo, or jo ... desto.

exercises.answer: Dette er den beste filmen jeg har sett.
exercises.en: This is the best film I have seen.

sections.title: Word order
sections.summary: Norwegian main clauses obey the V2 rule: the finite verb is always the second element, so starting a sentence with 'today' or 'then' pushes the subject behind the verb. Subordinate clauses behave differently, with ikke and other sentence adverbs placed before the verb.

rules.title: The basic sentence
rules.body: A neutral statement runs subject, verb, object, like English: Jeg spiser fisk. Hun leser avisen. Adverbs such as ikke, aldri, alltid, ofte, også and bare come straight after the finite verb: Jeg spiser ikke kjøtt. Hun leser alltid avisen. Expressions of manner, place and time typically go at the end, in that order: Vi spiser middag hjemme klokka seks.

examples.target: Vi spiser middag hjemme klokka seks.
examples.en: We eat dinner at home at six.

rules.title: The V2 rule: the verb is always second
rules.body: In a main clause the finite verb must be the second element. Whatever starts the sentence (the subject, a time expression, a place, an object, a whole subordinate clause), the verb comes next, and if the first element is not the subject, the subject moves to third place: I dag spiser jeg fisk. Nå kommer bussen. Det vet jeg ikke. Avisen leser jeg hver dag. Putting something other than the subject first is very common in Norwegian, so you will use inversion constantly.

examples.target: I morgen reiser vi til Bergen.

rules.title: Inversion after a fronted subordinate clause
rules.body: A subordinate clause placed at the start counts as the first element, so the main clause verb follows it immediately and the subject comes after the verb: Hvis det regner, blir jeg hjemme. Når jeg kommer hjem, spiser jeg middag. Fordi han var syk, kom han ikke. If the subordinate clause comes last instead, the main clause keeps normal order: Jeg blir hjemme hvis det regner.

examples.target: Hvis det regner, blir jeg hjemme.
examples.en: If it rains, I will stay at home.

examples.target: Når jeg kommer hjem, spiser jeg middag.
examples.en: When I get home, I eat dinner.

examples.target: Jeg blir hjemme hvis det regner.
examples.en: I will stay at home if it rains.

rules.title: Two verbs: the finite verb is second, the rest later
rules.body: When the sentence has a modal or an auxiliary, only the finite verb obeys V2; the infinitive or participle comes after the subject and any sentence adverb: Jeg kan ikke komme. Jeg har ikke sett ham. Nå må vi gå. I går kunne jeg ikke sove. The pattern is: (first element) finite verb, subject, ikke, other verb, object: I dag kan jeg ikke spise fisk.

examples.target: Jeg kan ikke komme i morgen.

examples.en: I have not seen the film.

examples.target: I dag kan jeg ikke spise fisk.

rules.title: Subordinate clauses: ikke before the verb
rules.body: Subordinate clauses are introduced by words like at (that), fordi (because), hvis (if), når (when), da (when, past), om (whether), som (who, which), selv om (even though), mens (while), før (before), etter at (after). Inside them the order is fixed: conjunction, subject, sentence adverb, verb. So ikke, aldri, alltid and friends move in front of the verb: Jeg vet at han ikke kommer. Hun sier at hun aldri drikker kaffe. Det er bra at du alltid er ærlig. There is never inversion inside a subordinate clause.

examples.target: Jeg vet at han ikke kommer.
examples.en: I know that he is not coming.

examples.target: Hun sier at hun aldri drikker kaffe.
examples.en: She says that she never drinks coffee.

examples.target: Vi blir hjemme fordi det regner.
examples.en: We are staying at home because it is raining.

examples.target: Jeg vet ikke hvorfor han ikke kom.
examples.en: I do not know why he did not come.

rules.title: Coordinating conjunctions keep main-clause order
rules.body: og (and), men (but), eller (or), for (because) and så (so) join two main clauses, and the clause after them keeps ordinary main-clause order with ikke after the verb: Jeg er trett, men jeg kan ikke sove. Compare for and fordi, which both mean because: Jeg blir hjemme, for jeg er ikke frisk (main clause after for) versus Jeg blir hjemme fordi jeg ikke er frisk (subordinate clause after fordi).

examples.target: Jeg er trett, men jeg kan ikke sove.
examples.en: I am tired, but I cannot sleep.

examples.target: Jeg blir hjemme, for jeg er ikke frisk.
examples.en: I am staying at home, because I am not well.

examples.target: Jeg blir hjemme fordi jeg ikke er frisk.
examples.en: I am staying at home because I am not well.

rules.title: Pronoun objects and ikke
rules.body: A noun object comes after ikke: Jeg liker ikke maten. Jeg så ikke mannen. But an unstressed pronoun object slips in before ikke: Jeg liker den ikke. Jeg så ham ikke. Jeg kjenner henne ikke. If the pronoun is stressed or contrasted it stays after ikke: Jeg så ikke HAM, jeg så broren hans. With an indirect object, it precedes the direct object: Jeg ga henne boka, or with til: Jeg ga boka til henne.

examples.en: I do not like the food.

rules.title: Relative clauses with som
rules.body: som (who, which, that) introduces relative clauses and is followed by subordinate word order: Mannen som bor der, er lege. Boka som jeg leser, er spennende. som is required when it is the subject of the relative clause (Mannen som bor der) and may be dropped when it is the object (Boka (som) jeg leser). A sentence adverb goes before the verb: Folk som ikke liker fisk, kan få kjøtt.

examples.target: Mannen som bor der, er lege.
examples.en: The man who lives there is a doctor.
The book I am reading is exciting.

examples.target: Folk som ikke liker fisk, kan få kjøtt.
examples.en: People who do not like fish can have meat.

rules.title: Questions and commands
rules.body: Yes/no questions put the finite verb first and the subject second: Kommer du? Kan du hjelpe meg? Question words take first place and the verb follows: Hvor bor du? (see chapter 8). Commands use the imperative, the infinitive without its final -e: Kom! Spis! Vent her! Verbs without -e keep their form: Gå! Se! A negative command puts ikke first: Ikke rør! Ikke gjør det!

sections.title: Questions and negation
sections.summary: Norwegian asks yes/no questions by putting the verb first, uses hva, hvem, hvor and hvorfor for open questions, and has a special word jo for saying yes to a negative question. This chapter also covers ikke, ingen, aldri and the other negative words.

rules.title: Yes/no questions: verb first
rules.body: To ask a yes/no question, put the finite verb first and the subject second. There is no helper verb like English 'do': Snakker du norsk? (Do you speak Norwegian?), Er du sulten? (Are you hungry?), Har du barn?, Kan du hjelpe meg?, Kommer hun i kveld? With two verbs, only the finite one moves: Har du spist? Skal vi gå?

rules.title: Question words
rules.body: The main question words are hva (what), hvem (who), hvor (where), når (when), hvorfor (why), hvordan (how), and hvilken, hvilket, hvilke (which, agreeing with the noun: hvilken bil, hvilket hus, hvilke bøker). hvor also combines with adjectives: hvor mye (how much), hvor mange (how many), hvor lenge (how long), hvor gammel (how old), hvor langt (how far). hva slags means 'what kind of'. The question word comes first, then the verb, then the subject: Hvor bor du? Hva heter du? Hvorfor kommer du ikke?

examples.en: How many children do you have?
Which house do you live in?

rules.title: hvem and hva as the subject
rules.body: When the question word itself is the subject, the verb follows it directly: Hvem kommer? (Who is coming?), Hva skjer? (What is happening?). In an indirect question where hvem or hva is the subject, Norwegian inserts som after it: Jeg vet ikke hvem som kommer. Vet du hva som skjer? Without som the sentence is wrong. When the question word is the object there is no som: Jeg vet ikke hvem hun møtte.

examples.target: Jeg vet ikke hvem som kommer.
examples.en: I do not know who is coming.
Do you know what is happening?

examples.target: Jeg vet ikke hvem hun møtte.
examples.en: I do not know whom she met.

rules.title: Answering: ja, nei and jo
rules.body: ja means yes and nei means no. After a negative question, an affirmative answer is jo, not ja: Liker du ikke fisk? Jo, jeg liker fisk! (Yes, I do!). Short answers often repeat the verb with det: Er du trett? Ja, det er jeg. Nei, det er jeg ikke. Snakker du norsk? Ja, det gjør jeg. Kan du svømme? Nei, det kan jeg ikke.

examples.target: Liker du ikke fisk? Jo, det gjør jeg!
examples.en: Don't you like fish? Yes, I do!

examples.target: Er du trett? Nei, det er jeg ikke.
examples.en: Are you tired? No, I am not.

examples.target: Snakker du norsk? Ja, det gjør jeg.
examples.en: Do you speak Norwegian? Yes, I do.

rules.title: Negation with ikke
rules.body: ikke (not) negates a sentence. In a main clause it comes right after the finite verb: Jeg forstår ikke. Han spiser ikke kjøtt. Jeg kan ikke svømme. Jeg har ikke sett den. In a subordinate clause it moves in front of the verb: ... at jeg ikke forstår. Before an infinitive with å, both ikke å and å ikke are accepted: Han lovet å ikke komme for sent. With a modal, må ikke means must not, while trenger ikke means need not: Du må ikke røyke her. Du trenger ikke komme.

examples.en: You do not need to come.

rules.title: Other negative words
rules.body: aldri means never: Jeg har aldri vært i Tromsø. ingen means no, nobody, none and agrees like an adjective: ingen (masculine, feminine and plural), intet or ikke noe (neuter); ingenting means nothing. Ingen kom. Jeg har ingen penger. Jeg har ingenting. ingen equals ikke noen, and in one position only the long form works: after a participle or infinitive you must say ikke noen or ikke noe, not ingen: Jeg har ikke sett noen (not: Jeg har sett ingen). Other useful negatives: ikke lenger (no longer), ennå ikke or ikke ennå (not yet), heller ikke (not either), verken ... eller (neither ... nor).

examples.target: Jeg har aldri vært i Tromsø.
examples.en: I have never been to Tromsø.

examples.target: Hun drikker verken kaffe eller te.
examples.en: She drinks neither coffee nor tea.

rules.title: Tags and softeners
rules.body: To check agreement, add ikke sant? (isn't it, right?) at the end of a statement: Du kommer, ikke sant? The small words vel and da soften or nudge: Du kommer vel? (You're coming, I hope?), Kom da! (Come on!). eller? at the end of a question makes it more open: Er du sulten, eller? To ask someone to repeat, say Unnskyld? or Hva sa du? rather than a bare Hva?

rules.title: Indirect questions
rules.body: An indirect yes/no question is introduced by om (whether, if): Jeg lurer på om hun kommer. Vet du om butikken er åpen? Indirect open questions keep the question word but use subordinate order, subject before verb and ikke before the verb: Vet du hvor hun bor? (not: hvor bor hun). Jeg vet ikke hvorfor han ikke kom. Remember som when hvem or hva is the subject: Vet du hvem som ringte?

examples.target: Jeg lurer på om hun kommer.
examples.en: I wonder whether she is coming.
Do you know where she lives?

examples.target: Jeg vet ikke hvorfor han ikke kom.
examples.en: I do not know why he did not come.

rules.title: hvilken and hva slags
rules.body: 'Which' agrees with the noun: hvilken bil (masculine or feminine), hvilket hus (neuter), hvilke bøker (plural). hva slags (what kind of) is followed by the bare noun: Hva slags musikk liker du? For 'what ... like', use hvordan: Hvordan er været? (What is the weather like?). Note that hva asks about things, hvem about people: Hvem er det? (Who is it?), Hva er det? (What is it?).

examples.en: What kind of music do you like?
What is the weather like today?

exercises.explain: ingen is equivalent to ikke noen.

After a participle you must use ikke noen; ingen is not allowed there.

exercises.explain: ikke sant? is the all-purpose question tag.

exercises.explain: When hvem or hva is the subject of an indirect question, som must follow it.

options: Jeg vet ikke hvorfor han ikke kom.

exercises.explain: Indirect questions take subordinate order with ikke before the verb.
Neither ... nor is verken ... eller.

exercises.explain: hva asks about things; for a person use hvem: Hvem er det?

sections.title: Prepositions and expressions of place and time
sections.summary: The small words i, på, til and hos carry most of the work of saying where and when, and their use often differs from English. This chapter sorts out place prepositions, the time expressions i dag and om morgenen, durations, and the prepositions that go with common verbs.

rules.title: i or på for places
rules.body: i (in) is used with countries, most cities, and enclosed spaces: i Norge, i Oslo, i stua, i huset, i bilen, i butikken. på (on, at) is used with surfaces, islands, and with institutions and places of activity: på bordet, på gulvet, på Svalbard, på skolen, på jobb, på kino, på kafé, på hotellet, på stasjonen, på sykehuset, på toalettet, and, oddly, på kjøkkenet and på badet. Inland Norwegian towns usually take på (på Lillehammer, på Hamar, på Gjøvik) while coastal ones take i (i Bergen, i Stavanger). The rule has many exceptions, so note the preposition each time you meet a new place word.

examples.en: The book is on the table.

rules.title: til, fra and hos
rules.body: til (to) marks direction towards a place or a person: Jeg reiser til Bergen. Vi går til stasjonen. Gi den til meg. fra (from) marks origin: Jeg kommer fra England. Toget fra Oslo. hos (at the home or premises of, like French chez) is used with people: hos legen (at the doctor's), hos Kari (at Kari's place), hos oss (at our place), hos frisøren. til also expresses possession in everyday speech: boka til Per (Per's book), bilen til naboen.

examples.target: Jeg reiser til Bergen i morgen.
examples.en: I am travelling to Bergen tomorrow.
We are having dinner at grandma's.

rules.title: Motion and location: hjem and hjemme
rules.body: Going somewhere normally takes til, being there takes i or på. But places that take på keep it for motion too: Jeg går på skolen (I go to school), Vi drar på kino, Han går på jobb. Several adverbs of place have a short form for movement and a longer one for location: hjem/hjemme (home, at home), ut/ute (out, outside), inn/inne (in, inside), opp/oppe (up), ned/nede (down), bort/borte (away), hit/her (here), dit/der (there). Jeg går hjem. Jeg er hjemme. Kom hit! Jeg er her.

rules.title: Other place prepositions
rules.body: under (under), over (over, above), ved (by, at), ved siden av (next to), foran (in front of), bak (behind), mellom (between), utenfor (outside), innenfor (inside), rundt (around), gjennom (through), langs (along), mot (towards, against), fra ... til (from ... to). Nøklene ligger på bordet ved døra. Bilen står foran huset. Note that Norwegian often uses a posture verb where English says 'is': ligger (lies) for flat things, står (stands) for upright things, sitter (sits), henger (hangs).

examples.en: The car is (standing) in front of the house.

examples.target: Banken ligger ved siden av posten.
examples.en: The bank is next to the post office.
The cat is sleeping under the table.

rules.title: Time: i dag, i morgen, om morgenen
rules.body: i is used for today, tomorrow and the current or recent period: i dag (today), i morgen (tomorrow), i går (yesterday), i kveld (tonight), i natt (last night or tonight), i morges (this morning), i år, i fjor (last year), i sommer, i helgen. om is used for habitual parts of the day and seasons: om morgenen (in the mornings), om kvelden, om natten, om sommeren, om vinteren. Days of the week take på for one occasion: på mandag (on Monday); habit is om mandagene or på mandager. Months take i: i januar. Clock times take klokka with no preposition: klokka åtte.

examples.en: I drink coffee in the mornings.

rules.title: Durations, 'ago', 'since' and 'until'
rules.body: i + a length of time means 'for': Jeg har bodd her i tre år. på + a length of time means 'within', the time it took: Jeg gjorde det på en time (I did it in an hour). om + a length of time means 'in', counting forward from now: Vi reiser om to dager (in two days' time). for ... siden means 'ago': for to år siden. siden means 'since': siden 2010, siden i går. til means 'until': fra ni til fem, til mandag. In negative sentences 'for' becomes på: Jeg har ikke sett ham på to år.

examples.target: Jeg har bodd her i tre år.
examples.en: I have lived here for three years.
We are leaving in two days.

examples.target: Jeg flyttet hit for to år siden.
examples.en: I moved here two years ago.

examples.target: Butikken er åpen fra ni til fem.
examples.en: The shop is open from nine to five.

rules.title: Verbs and adjectives with fixed prepositions
rules.body: Many verbs and adjectives come with a preposition that must be learned with them: snakke med (talk to), snakke om (talk about), tenke på (think of), vente på (wait for), se på (look at), høre på (listen to), lete etter (look for), spørre om (ask about), be om (ask for), tro på (believe in), glede seg til (look forward to), være glad i (be fond of, love), være redd for (be afraid of), være interessert i (be interested in), ha lyst på (feel like, with a noun), ha lyst til å (feel like, with a verb).

examples.en: I am waiting for the bus.
I am looking forward to the weekend.

rules.title: Prepositions at the end
rules.body: As in spoken English, Norwegian puts the preposition at the end of questions and relative clauses rather than in front of the question word: Hva tenker du på? (What are you thinking about?), Hvem snakker du med?, Hvor kommer du fra?, Huset jeg bor i (the house I live in), Mannen hun venter på. This is the normal, correct order, not a colloquialism.

examples.target: Dette er huset jeg bor i.
examples.en: This is the house I live in.

rules.title: Fixed phrases with i and på
rules.body: Some expressions must be learned whole: på norsk (in Norwegian), på TV, på internett, på telefonen, på vei (on the way), på ferie (on holiday), på tur (on a trip or hike), på besøk (visiting), på fest (at a party), på landet (in the countryside), i byen (in town), i live (alive), i stedet (instead), i hvert fall (at any rate), i det hele tatt (at all). Jeg har vært på tur i fjellet. Hva heter det på norsk?

examples.en: What is it called in Norwegian?

examples.en: We are going on holiday in July.

exercises.explain: Inland towns like Lillehammer, Hamar and Gjøvik take på; coastal cities take i.

sections.title: Numbers, time, dates and polite phrases
sections.summary: Norwegian has two ways of saying numbers above twenty, tells the half hours in a way that trips up English speakers, and has a rich set of takk expressions with no single word for please. This chapter covers counting, klokka, dates and everyday politeness.

rules.title: Numbers 0 to 20
rules.body: null, en (ett), to, tre, fire, fem, seks, sju (or syv), åtte, ni, ti, elleve, tolv, tretten, fjorten, femten, seksten, sytten, atten, nitten, tjue (or tyve). 'One' agrees with the noun: en bil, ei (or en) jente, ett hus, ett år. sju and tjue are the official forms from 1951, but syv and tyve are still widely used in speech, especially in Oslo and in conservative Bokmål; both are correct.

examples.target: Jeg har to brødre og ei søster.
examples.en: I have two brothers and one sister.

rules.title: Tens and the two counting systems
rules.body: The tens are tjue, tretti, førti, femti, seksti, sytti, åtti, nitti; then hundre, tusen, en million. In the modern system, introduced in 1951 and used in all official contexts, the tens come first: tjueen (21), tjueto, trettifem (35), femtiåtte (58). In the older system, still common in everyday speech, the units come first with og: enogtyve (21), toogtyve, femogtredve (35), åtteogfemti (58). Learn to say the modern system and to understand both. Larger numbers use og before the final part: hundre og en (101), to hundre og femti (250), ett tusen ni hundre og nittifire (1994).

rules.title: Ordinal numbers
rules.body: første (1st), andre (2nd), tredje (3rd), fjerde (4th), femte, sjette, sjuende (or syvende), åttende, niende, tiende, ellevte, tolvte, trettende, fjortende, femtende, sekstende, syttende, attende, nittende, tjuende, tjueførste (21st), trettiende, hundrede. In figures an ordinal is written with a full stop: 1. etasje (first floor), 17. mai, den 3. juni. Ordinals are used with the definite article: den første dagen, det andre huset.

examples.en: the 17th of May, Norway's national day
She lives on the third floor.

rules.title: Telling the time
rules.body: Hva er klokka? Klokka er åtte (It is eight o'clock). 'At eight' is simply klokka åtte, with no preposition. Minutes past use over and minutes to use på: fem over åtte (8:05), ti på ni (8:50), kvart over åtte (8:15), kvart på ni (8:45). The half hour looks forward to the next hour: halv ni means 8:30, not 9:30. Minutes near the half hour are counted from it: fem på halv ni (8:25), fem over halv ni (8:35). Timetables use the 24-hour clock written with a full stop: 20.30, read as tjue tretti.

examples.en: The train leaves at a quarter to ten.

rules.title: Days, months and dates
rules.body: Days and months are written with a small letter: mandag, tirsdag, onsdag, torsdag, fredag, lørdag, søndag; januar, februar, mars, april, mai, juni, juli, august, september, oktober, november, desember. A date is day then month: 17. mai, read syttende mai; den 3. juni, read den tredje juni. In figures the order is day.month.year: 17.05.2024. Years are read in hundreds up to 1999 (1814: atten hundre og fjorten) and as thousands from 2000 (2024: to tusen og tjuefire, or in speech tjuetjuefire). Hvilken dato er det i dag? Det er den syttende mai.

examples.target: Hvilken dato er det i dag?

rules.title: Age, prices and quantities
rules.body: Age: Hvor gammel er du? Jeg er tretti år (gammel). Prices: Hva koster det? or Hvor mye koster det? Det koster femti kroner. The currency is en krone, plural kroner, abbreviated kr; one krone has 100 øre, though coins below one krone no longer exist. Times: en gang (once), to ganger (twice), tre ganger i uka (three times a week). Halves: en halv time (half an hour), halvannen time (an hour and a half), halvparten av (half of), et kvarter (a quarter of an hour). Approximations: cirka, omtrent, rundt (about).

examples.target: Jeg trener tre ganger i uka.
examples.en: I train three times a week.
It takes an hour and a half.

rules.title: takk and its many uses
rules.body: takk (thanks) is combined with almost anything: takk skal du ha and tusen takk (thank you very much), mange takk, takk for hjelpen (thanks for the help), takk for i dag (thanks for today, said when parting after a shared day), takk for sist (thanks for last time, said when you meet someone again), takk for meg (thanks for having me, said by a guest when leaving). After every meal you say takk for maten to the cook or host, who answers vel bekomme. ja takk and nei takk are yes please and no thank you. Replies to thanks: bare hyggelig (my pleasure), ingen årsak (no problem), vær så god.

examples.en: Good to see you again! (thanks for last time)
Thank you so much for the help.
No thank you, I am full.

rules.title: vær så god and asking politely
rules.body: Norwegian has no single word for 'please'. vær så god means 'here you are' when handing something over, 'go ahead' when inviting someone to start, and 'you're welcome' in reply to thanks. To ask politely, use a question with kan or kunne: Kan jeg få en kaffe? (Can I have a coffee?), Kunne du hjelpe meg? (Could you help me?), often with takk at the end: En kaffe, takk. Adding er du snill (if you would be so kind) or vær så snill makes a request softer or more pleading: Lukk døra, er du snill.

examples.en: Here you are! / Go ahead! / You're welcome!
Can I have the bill, please?

rules.title: Greetings and small talk
rules.body: hei is the universal greeting, and hei hei or ha det (bra) means goodbye. More formal: god morgen, god dag, god kveld, god natt. Hyggelig å hilse på deg (nice to meet you), vi ses (see you), ha en fin dag (have a nice day). The usual 'how are you' is Hvordan går det? or Hvordan har du det?, answered Bare bra, takk, or Det går bra. unnskyld is used for excuse me and sorry; beklager is sorry for something you regret. Norwegians say hei to shop staff and bus drivers and do not use titles or surnames in everyday address.
